About: The Cyclotron — The Clock That Does Not Care How Fast

Source

Lecture
Magnetic force on moving charges — the cyclotron
Simulation
Cyclotron: fixed-frequency oscillator, spiralling proton, per-lap timer
Concept
The orbital period T = 2πm/(qB) contains no v — so a fixed-frequency drive stays in step as the orbit grows.
Serves
Lorentz force does no work; T is v-independent; resonance condition ω_drive = ω_c.
Inquiry
As the proton speeds up, does the time for one lap shorten, lengthen, or stay the same?
Misconception
"A faster particle must go round faster" — the longer path and higher speed cancel exactly.

Guided Inquiry

1 · The machine

Two D-shaped metal electrodes — the dees — sit in a uniform magnetic field B pointing out of the page. A narrow gap separates them, and an alternating voltage of peak value V is applied across that gap. A proton of charge q and mass m starts near the centre.

2 · One lap at twice the speed

A charged particle travels in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. Its speed is now doubled, with the field unchanged. The time to go once round the new circle is:

3 · Where the energy enters

Inside a dee the field is purely magnetic; the only electric field is in the gap. Over one lap, where does the proton's kinetic energy change?

4 · One fixed frequency

The oscillator across the gap runs at a single frequency and is never retuned, yet it accelerates the proton on every crossing for the whole climb. That frequency is:

5 · How much energy comes out

Two cyclotrons are identical except for the gap voltage: one at 8 kV, one at 60 kV. Each proton climbs until its orbit fills the dees, radius R. Compare the two exit energies.

6 · Out of step

The drive frequency is offset from fc by a few per cent, with B unchanged. Over the following laps the proton:

The Cyclotron

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A proton circles between two D-shaped electrodes in a magnetic field and is kicked forward by an alternating voltage across the gap between them. The sim times each lap and tracks the radius, the speed and the energy, and you can set the field, the gap voltage and the drive frequency. This is the cyclotron.

What you'll learn

  • What the magnetic field does inside the dees, and what the voltage across the gap does.
  • What sets the rhythm of the machine, and what limits the energy it finally delivers.
  • What happens when the drive is not matched to the proton.
Two dees with a narrow gap, a field B out of the page (the dots), and a proton near the centre.

What's on screen

  • The dees: two D-shaped electrodes with a narrow gap between them. The faint dots mark B pointing out of the page.
  • The gap voltage: the + and − beside the gap swap every half-lap, and a red or cyan flash marks each crossing.
  • The proton: a teal trail behind it, a dashed line for its radius r, and a bar for the scale in cm.
  • Live readouts: the measured lap time, laps completed, r, v, the cyclotron frequency fc and the kinetic energy K.
See itStart the proton with B = 0.50 T and V = 8 kV. Watch for: the trail spiralling outward, the laps counter climbing and the radius r growing from 2.09 cm.

Fixed: the particle is a proton, it starts at 1.00 × 10⁶ m/s, and the dees have a set radius of about 12.5 cm. On screen, time is slowed by about 4 million, so one lap at 0.50 T takes about half a second at 1× speed.

03

The magnetic field turns the proton and the gap speeds it up

Inside a dee there is only the magnetic field. Its force F⃗ = q v⃗ × B⃗ is always at right angles to the motion, so it does no work: the speed and the kinetic energy stay fixed while the proton turns through a half circle.

The electric field exists only in the narrow gap. Each time the proton crosses it, the voltage across the gap adds energy:

ΔK = qV per crossing, 2qV per lap
The gap gives all the energy. The dees only steer.

With V = 8 kV and q = e, each crossing adds 8 keV, so the proton's 5.22 keV becomes 13.22 keV after the first crossing and 21.22 keV after the second.

See itRun the proton with V = 8 kV at Speed 0.25×. Watch for: K holding steady inside a dee, then jumping by 8.00 keV at each flash in the gap.
04

Every lap takes the same time as the orbit grows

On a circle the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force, m v² / r = q v B, so the radius grows in proportion to the speed. The lap time is that circumference divided by that speed, and v cancels:

r = m v / (q B)    T = 2π m / (q B)
T contains no v.

A faster proton goes round a bigger circle, in exact proportion, so each lap takes the same time. At B = 0.50 T that time is T = 131.19 ns, which is the lap time the sim measures. Over the climb, v rises from 1.00 × 10⁶ to 6.00 × 10⁶ m/s and r from 2.09 cm to 12.53 cm, while T does not move.

See itRun the default proton with B = 0.50 T and V = 8 kV. Watch for: the measured lap time reading 131.19 ns on every lap while r grows.
05

One fixed frequency stays in step for the whole climb

The proton needs the gap voltage to flip once per half-lap. Since the lap time never changes, one oscillator frequency matches it at every radius:

fc = q B / (2π m)  =  1 / T
The cyclotron frequency. Set the drive to it and leave it alone.

At B = 0.50 T, fc = 7.62 MHz. It depends only on the particle and the field: at 1.00 T it doubles to 15.25 MHz. The sim sets the drive to fc when detune is zero, and the line at the bottom right of the picture shows both numbers. The drive is never retuned during a run, yet every crossing finds the gap field pointing the right way.

See itSet B = 1.00 T with V = 8 kV. Watch for: fc reading 15.25 MHz, the bottom-right line showing the same drive, and K still rising at every crossing.
06

The exit energy comes from B and the size of the machine

The orbit grows until it fills the dees, at radius R. There the speed is v = qBR / m, so the final energy is

Kmax = (q B R)² / (2 m)
No V appears.

With the sim's R of about 12.5 cm and B = 0.50 T, Kmax = 187.91 keV. Doubling B to 1.00 T gives four times as much, 751.66 keV. The gap voltage only sets the number of turns: V = 8 kV needs 23 crossings, V = 60 kV needs 4, and both leave at the same energy.

See itSet V = 60 kV with B = 0.50 T. Watch for: the orbit filling the dees within a few laps and the banner reading 187.91 keV, the same as at 8 kV.
07

A mismatched drive falls out of step

If the drive frequency is off by a fraction δ = Δf/fc, the gap voltage arrives a little late (or early) at every crossing, and the slip adds up crossing after crossing. The gain per crossing then shrinks:

ΔKn = qV cos[(n − ½) π δ]
n counts crossings from the start of the run. At δ = 0 every gain is the full qV.

At δ = +5% the gain falls from 7.98 keV at the first crossing to nearly zero at the tenth, and from the eleventh crossing the gap decelerates the proton. K peaks near 56 keV, then falls back toward zero and the sim shows Out of step. The proton never reaches Kmax. A negative offset does the same.

See itSet the detune to +5.0% with B = 0.50 T and V = 8 kV. Watch for: the flash turning from red to cyan after about ten crossings, then K falling and the banner Out of step.
08

Where it matters

  • Isotope production. Cyclotrons accelerate protons to hit a target, and this is how many of the short-lived isotopes used in medical scanning are made.
  • Design rule. Kmax grows as B²R², so a stronger magnet or a larger dee radius raises the beam energy. The gap voltage does not.
  • The limit. The sim keeps the proton's mass fixed. In a real machine the mass grows with speed, about 1% by K ≈ 9.4 MeV for a proton, so T lengthens and one fixed frequency falls behind. Larger machines then vary the frequency or the field.
09

Summary

In one line. A cyclotron pairs a magnetic field that steers a proton with an alternating voltage that drives it, and the two must work together.

Key points

  • T = 2π m / (q B) and fc = q B / (2π m) do not depend on v.
  • The gap adds qV per crossing. The magnetic field adds none.
  • Kmax = (q B R)² / 2m has no V in it. V sets only the number of turns.
  • A drive offset by δ makes the gain per crossing shrink, then reverse.

Common mix-ups

  • "A faster proton must go round faster." Its circle grows in proportion, so the lap time stays the same.
  • "A bigger gap voltage gives a higher exit energy." It only gets there in fewer turns. B and R set the limit.

Things to try on your own

  • Run B = 0.20 T, then 1.50 T, and read K at extraction in each.
  • Try detune +2.0%, then +10.0%, and compare how soon the flash turns cyan.
  • Set V = 5 kV and count the laps needed to fill the dees.
